Question_Text: I _________ going to visit my grandmother.
Detailed_Solution: The pronoun 'I' always takes the helping verb 'am' in the near future.

Question_Text: Kato _________ going to board the bus.
Detailed_Solution: Kato is a singular subject, so we use 'is'.

Question_Text: We _________ going to have a big bash.
Detailed_Solution: 'We' is a plural subject, so it requires the helping verb 'are'.

Question_Text: Identify the correct structure for a future plan.
Detailed_Solution: The correct formula is Subject + am/is/are + going to + verb.

Question_Text: The holiday _________ going to commence in August.
Detailed_Solution: The holiday is singular, so 'is' is the correct helping verb.

Question_Text: Babirye and Kato _________ going to help their parents.
Detailed_Solution: There are two people (plural), so use 'are'.

Question_Text: It _________ going to rain this afternoon.
Detailed_Solution: 'It' takes the singular helping verb 'is'.

Question_Text: You _________ going to enjoy the rural area.
Detailed_Solution: The pronoun 'You' always takes 'are' in this structure.

Question_Text: They _________ going to vacate the house.
Detailed_Solution: 'They' is plural and requires 'are'.

Question_Text: My relatives _________ going to arrive tomorrow.
Detailed_Solution: 'Relatives' is plural, so we use 'are'.

Question_Text: Choose the correct verb form: We are going to _________ our notes.
Detailed_Solution: After 'going to', we use the base form (infinitive) of the verb.

Question_Text: Kiki is going to _________ a delicious cake.
Detailed_Solution: The verb after 'going to' must be in its simplest form.

Question_Text: The travellers are _________ to board the train.
Detailed_Solution: The near future structure always uses the participle 'going'.

Question_Text: Is she _________ to pay the bus fare?
Detailed_Solution: Even in questions, the structure 'going to' remains the same.

Question_Text: Which sentence describes a plan that has already been decided?
Option_C: I am going to visit the farm.
Detailed_Solution: 'Going to' is used for intentions and plans already made.

Question_Text: Complete: Polly is going to _________ to London.
Detailed_Solution: Use the base verb 'fly' after 'going to'.

Question_Text: Complete: Are you _________ to help mother?
Detailed_Solution: The continuous form 'going' is required here.

Question_Text: I _________ going to prepare for my vacation.
Detailed_Solution: Subject-verb agreement: I + am.

Question_Text: The headteacher is going to _________ the pupils.
Detailed_Solution: Base form 'address' follows 'going to'.

Question_Text: Manya and friends are _________ to spend the holiday together.
Detailed_Solution: The structure is 'are going to'.

Question_Text: Rewrite using 'going to': I shall visit my parents.
Option_B: I am going to visit my parents.
Option_C: I going to visit my parents.
Option_D: I am going visit my parents.
Detailed_Solution: When changing 'shall' to 'going to', you must add 'am'.

Question_Text: Rewrite using 'going to': The girls will fetch water.
Option_A: The girls is going to fetch water.
Option_B: The girls are going to fetch water.
Option_C: The girls going to fetch water.
Option_D: The girls will going to fetch water.
Detailed_Solution: 'Will' is replaced by 'are going to' because 'girls' is plural.

Question_Text: Rewrite using 'going to': She will spend the holidays with relatives.
Option_A: She going to spend the holidays.
Option_B: She is going to spend the holidays with relatives.
Option_C: She am going to spend the holidays.
Option_D: She are going to spend the holidays.
Detailed_Solution: Singular subject 'She' needs 'is going to'.

Question_Text: Rewrite using 'going to': We shall revise our books.
Option_A: We are going to revise our books.
Option_B: We is going to revise our books.
Option_C: We going to revise our books.
Option_D: We shall going to revise our books.
Detailed_Solution: 'Shall' becomes 'are going to' for the subject 'We'.

Question_Text: Rewrite using 'going to': He will help his parents on the farm.
Option_A: He is going to help his parents on the farm.
Option_B: He are going to help his parents.
Option_C: He am going to help his parents.
Option_D: He going to help his parents.
Detailed_Solution: Correct transformation of 'will' to 'is going to'.

Question_Text: Rewrite using 'going to': They will write to their pen-pals.
Option_A: They are going to write to their pen-pals.
Option_B: They is going to write to their pen-pals.
Option_C: They am going to write to their pen-pals.
Option_D: They will going to write to their pen-pals.
Detailed_Solution: 'They' (plural) takes 'are going to'.

Question_Text: Rewrite using 'going to': The new term will commence next week.
Option_A: The new term is going to commence next week.
Option_B: The new term are going to commence.
Option_C: The new term am going to commence.
Option_D: The new term going to commence.
Detailed_Solution: 'The new term' is a singular concept, so use 'is going to'.

Question_Text: Rewrite using 'going to': Nambi will travel to Kigali.
Option_C: Nambi is going to travel to Kigali.
Option_D: Nambi going to travel to Kigali.
Detailed_Solution: Proper noun Nambi (singular) takes 'is going to'.

Question_Text: Rewrite using 'going to': I shall enjoy my brother's birthday party.
Option_A: I is going to enjoy the party.
Option_B: I am going to enjoy my brother's birthday party.
Option_C: I are going to enjoy the party.
Option_D: I going to enjoy the party.
Detailed_Solution: Transformation of 'I shall' to 'I am going to'.

Question_Text: Rewrite using 'going to': The children will go to the zoo.
Option_A: The children are going to go to the zoo.
Option_B: The children is going to go to the zoo.
Option_C: The children am going to go to the zoo.
Option_D: The children going to go to the zoo.
Detailed_Solution: 'Children' is plural, so it requires 'are going to'.

Question_Text: Manya is a clever duck, ________?
Detailed_Solution: A positive statement needs a negative tag. 'Is' becomes 'isn't'.

Question_Text: Kiki cannot bark, ________?
Detailed_Solution: A negative statement needs a positive tag. 'Cannot' becomes 'can'.

Question_Text: We are going to the village, ________?
Detailed_Solution: The helping verb 'are' in a positive statement becomes 'aren't' in the tag.

Question_Text: You are not a teacher, ________?
Detailed_Solution: The negative 'are not' becomes 'are' in the positive tag.

Question_Text: Polly can fly high, ________?
Detailed_Solution: Positive statement with 'can' takes a negative tag 'can't'.

Question_Text: The holiday is enjoyable, ________?
Detailed_Solution: The subject 'holiday' is replaced by the pronoun 'it'.

Question_Text: It is not raining, ________?
Detailed_Solution: Negative 'is not' moves to a positive 'is it?'.

Question_Text: They are our relatives, ________?
Detailed_Solution: Positive 'are' becomes negative 'aren't'.

Question_Text: The bus is slow, ________?
Detailed_Solution: Match the verb 'is' with 'isn't' and the object 'bus' with 'it'.

Question_Text: You have a pen-pal, ________?
Detailed_Solution: Using the helping verb 'have' to form a negative tag 'haven't'.

Question_Text: They went to the farm, ________?
Detailed_Solution: For past simple verbs without a helping verb, use 'did' or 'didn't'.

Question_Text: Kato will visit London, ________?
Detailed_Solution: 'Will' always changes to the negative contraction 'won't'.

Question_Text: We shall pass the exam, ________?
Detailed_Solution: 'Shall' changes to the negative contraction 'shan't'.

Question_Text: The term hasn't ended yet, ________?
Detailed_Solution: The negative 'hasn't' becomes the positive 'has'.

Question_Text: You didn't pay the fare, ________?
Detailed_Solution: Negative 'didn't' becomes positive 'did'.

Question_Text: He always comes here, ________?
Detailed_Solution: For present simple with singular subjects, use 'does' or 'doesn't'.

Question_Text: Manya waddles nicely, ________?
Detailed_Solution: Positive present tense (waddles) requires the tag 'doesn't he?'.

Question_Text: The kittens were playing, ________?
Detailed_Solution: Match 'were' with 'weren't' and 'kittens' with 'they'.

Question_Text: You don't like sugar, ________?
Detailed_Solution: Negative 'don't' becomes positive 'do'.

Question_Text: The trip was very long, ________?
Detailed_Solution: Past tense 'was' becomes 'wasn't'.

Question_Text: I am in Primary Seven, ________?
Detailed_Solution: PLE TRAP: 'I am' always takes the negative tag 'aren't I?'.

Question_Text: Let's go for vacation, ________?
Detailed_Solution: PLE TRAP: Suggestions starting with 'Let's' always take 'shall we?'.

Question_Text: Manya hardly eats meat, ________?
Detailed_Solution: PLE TRAP: 'Hardly' is a negative word, so the tag must be positive 'does he?'.

Question_Text: Open the classroom, ________?
Detailed_Solution: PLE TRAP: Commands or requests (imperatives) take 'will you?'.

Question_Text: I am not slow, ________?
Detailed_Solution: Unlike the positive 'I am', the negative 'I am not' takes the regular 'am I?'.

Question_Text: You'd rather stay, ________?
Detailed_Solution: 'You'd rather' is a contraction of 'You would rather', so the tag is 'wouldn't you?'.

Question_Text: You'd better go, ________?
Detailed_Solution: 'You'd better' is a contraction of 'You had better', so the tag is 'hadn't you?'.

Question_Text: There is a kitten in the kitchen, ________?
Detailed_Solution: Statements starting with 'There is' use 'there' in the tag.

Question_Text: Let us help our parents, ________?
Detailed_Solution: 'Let us' (even without the contraction 's) is a suggestion taking 'shall we?'.

Question_Text: He rarely comes here, ________?
Detailed_Solution: 'Rarely' is a semi-negative word; it requires a positive tag 'does he?'.

Question_Text: Complete the rule: Having + _________ participle.
Detailed_Solution: The word 'Having' is always followed by a Past Participle (V3) to show a completed action.

Question_Text: Having _________ our hands, we ate the food.
Detailed_Solution: 'Washed' is the past participle (V3) required after 'Having'.

Question_Text: _________ through the window, I saw a thief.
Detailed_Solution: Present participles (-ing) are used to describe an action happening at the same time as another.

Question_Text: Having _________ my bag, I boarded the bus.
Detailed_Solution: The action of packing was finished before boarding, so we use 'Having packed'.

Question_Text: _________ said her prayers, the old woman lay down.
Detailed_Solution: 'Having' is the correct participle to start a sentence showing a completed sequence.

Question_Text: Having _________ the letter, I went to the post office.
Detailed_Solution: 'Written' is the past participle (V3) of 'write'.

Question_Text: Having _________ the snake, the children ran away.
Detailed_Solution: 'Seen' is the V3 form required after 'Having'.

Question_Text: _________ the bell, the pupils ran for assembly.
Detailed_Solution: The action of hearing led immediately to the action of running.

Question_Text: Having _________ the chores, Kato went to play.
Detailed_Solution: 'Done' is the past participle of 'do'.

Question_Text: Having _________ the bus fare, I entered the coach.
Detailed_Solution: 'Paid' is the V3 form of 'pay'.

Question_Text: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
Detailed_Solution: Rule: Having + V3 (eaten). 'Ate' is V2, which is wrong here.

Question_Text: Choose the correct V3 form: Having _________ (take) my report card, I left.
Detailed_Solution: 'Taken' is the correct past participle of 'take'.

Question_Text: Complete the sentence: _________ for the journey, we said goodbye.
Detailed_Solution: 'Having prepared' shows that the preparation was finished before saying goodbye.

Question_Text: Having _________ (begin) the holiday, Manya felt happy.
Detailed_Solution: 'Begun' is the V3 form of 'begin'. 'Began' is V2.

Question_Text: Having _________ (buy) the stamps, she posted the letter.
Detailed_Solution: 'Bought' is the correct past participle of 'buy'.

Question_Text: Identify the participle in: 'Shouting loudly, the parrot flew away.'
Detailed_Solution: 'Shouting' is the present participle starting the phrase.

Question_Text: Having _________ (find) the pen-pal, he wrote a letter.
Detailed_Solution: 'Found' is the V3 form of 'find'.

Question_Text: Having _________ (speak) to Otim, I understood the plan.
Detailed_Solution: 'Spoken' is the V3 form of 'speak'.

Question_Text: Complete: _________ the bus, the driver started the engine.
Detailed_Solution: This shows one action completed before the next started.

Question_Text: Having _________ (spend) all my money, I walked home.
Detailed_Solution: 'Spent' is the correct past participle.

Question_Text: Join: He finished the chores. He went to the zoo. (Begin: Having...)
Option_A: Having finish the chores, he went to the zoo.
Option_B: Having finished the chores, he went to the zoo.
Option_C: Having finishing the chores, he went to the zoo.
Option_D: Having did the chores, he went to the zoo.
Detailed_Solution: The first action (finishing) must be in V3 after 'Having'.

Question_Text: Join: She saw the teacher. She hid under the desk. (Begin: Seeing...)
Option_A: Seeing the teacher, she hid under the desk.
Option_B: See the teacher, she hid under the desk.
Option_C: Seen the teacher, she hid under the desk.
Option_D: Having see the teacher, she hid under the desk.
Detailed_Solution: Using the present participle 'Seeing' shows the two actions happened almost instantly.

Question_Text: Join: Manya wrote the letter. He bought an envelope. (Begin: Having...)
Option_A: Having wrote the letter, he bought an envelope.
Option_B: Having writing the letter, he bought an envelope.
Option_C: Having written the letter, he bought an envelope.
Option_D: Having written the letter he bought an envelope.
Detailed_Solution: Note the comma after 'letter' and the correct V3 'written'.

Question_Text: Join: Kiki ate the fish. She felt sleepy. (Begin: Having...)
Option_A: Having eaten the fish, she felt sleepy.
Option_B: Having ate the fish, she felt sleepy.
Option_C: Having eat the fish, she felt sleepy.
Option_D: Eating the fish she felt sleepy.
Detailed_Solution: The past participle of 'eat' is 'eaten'.

Question_Text: Join: The term ended. We went up-country. (Begin: Having...)
Option_A: Having end the term, we went up-country.
Option_B: Having ended the term we went up-country.
Option_C: Having ending the term, we went up-country.
Option_D: Having ended the term, we went up-country.
Detailed_Solution: Correct V3 and correct use of the comma to separate the clauses.

Question_Text: Join: He received his report card. He showed it to dad. (Begin: After...)
Option_A: After receive his report card, he showed it to dad.
Option_B: After receiving his report card, he showed it to dad.
Option_C: After he have received his report card, he showed it to dad.
Option_D: After received his report card, he showed it to dad.
Detailed_Solution: After the preposition 'After', use the gerund/participle 'receiving'.

Question_Text: Join: Polly reached the village. She visited her relatives. (Begin: Having...)
Option_A: Having reaching the village, she visited her relatives.
Option_B: Having reached the village she visited her relatives.
Option_C: Having reached the village, she visited her relatives.
Option_D: Having reach the village, she visited her relatives.
Detailed_Solution: Past participle 'reached' is used after 'Having'.

Question_Text: Join: They cleaned the compound. They started the party. (Begin: Having...)
Option_A: Having clean the compound, they started the party.
Option_B: Having cleaned the compound, they started the party.
Option_C: Having cleaning the compound, they started the party.
Option_D: Having cleaned the compound they started the party.
Detailed_Solution: 'Cleaned' is the past participle; a comma is essential for the structure.

Question_Text: Join: He found the money. He took it to the teacher. (Begin: Having...)
Option_A: Having found the money, he took it to the teacher.
Option_B: Having find the money, he took it to the teacher.
Option_C: Having finded the money, he took it to the teacher.
Option_D: Finding the money he took it to the teacher.
Detailed_Solution: 'Found' is the correct V3 of 'find'.

Question_Text: Join: She woke up early. She caught the bus. (Begin: Having...)
Option_A: Having woken up early, she caught the bus.
Option_B: Having woke up early, she caught the bus.
Option_C: Having wake up early, she caught the bus.
Option_D: Having waking up early, she caught the bus.
Detailed_Solution: 'Woken' is the past participle of 'wake'. 'Woke' is only for past simple.

Question_Text: In reported speech, the word now changes to ________.
Detailed_Solution: The time word 'now' always shifts to 'then' when moving from direct to indirect speech.

Question_Text: In reported speech, today changes to ________.
Detailed_Solution: 'Today' shifts to 'that day' to show the time has passed.

Question_Text: The word tomorrow shifts to ________.
Detailed_Solution: 'Tomorrow' becomes 'the following day' or 'the next day'.

Question_Text: In reported speech, the verb am or is changes to ________.
Detailed_Solution: Present simple helping verbs shift to the past simple 'was'.

Question_Text: The word here changes to ________.
Detailed_Solution: Place words shift away from the speaker: 'here' becomes 'there'.

Question_Text: If the speaker is a boy, the pronoun I usually changes to ________.
Detailed_Solution: Pronouns must match the gender of the original speaker.

Question_Text: The quotation marks (   ) are ________ in reported speech.
Detailed_Solution: Reported speech is a statement, so we remove the original speech marks.

Question_Text: We in direct speech often changes to ________ in reported speech.
Detailed_Solution: Plural first-person pronouns shift to the third-person 'they'.

Question_Text: Shall or will shifts to ________.
Detailed_Solution: Future modals shift to the conditional 'would'.

Question_Text: Yesterday changes to ________.
Detailed_Solution: 'Yesterday' shifts back to 'the day before' or 'the previous day'.

Question_Text: Kato said, I am happy. Kato said that he ________ happy.
Detailed_Solution: Present simple 'am' shifts to past simple 'was'.

Question_Text: I will travel, said Polly. Polly said that she ________ travel.
Detailed_Solution: 'Will' always shifts to 'would' in reported speech.

Question_Text: They said, We are digging. They said that they ________ digging.
Detailed_Solution: Present continuous 'are' shifts to past continuous 'were'.

Question_Text: I have finished, said Kiki. Kiki said that she ________ finished.
Detailed_Solution: Present perfect 'have' shifts to past perfect 'had'.

Question_Text: Manya said, I am busy now. Manya said that he was busy ________.
Detailed_Solution: The word 'now' must be changed to 'then' in the reported version.

Question_Text: The teacher said, Water boils at 100°C. The teacher said that water ________ at 100°C.
Detailed_Solution: TRAP: Scientific facts do not change tense in reported speech.

Question_Text: We can swim, they said. They said that they ________ swim.
Detailed_Solution: The modal 'can' shifts to the past form 'could'.

Question_Text: It is raining today, said mom. Mom said that it was raining ________.
Detailed_Solution: Change 'today' to 'that day' to complete the transformation.

Question_Text: I must go, said Ali. Ali said that he ________ to go.
Detailed_Solution: 'Must' changes to 'had to' in reported speech.

Question_Text: I saw a lion, said the boy. The boy said that he ________ a lion.
Detailed_Solution: Past simple 'saw' shifts back to past perfect 'had seen'.

Question_Text: Rewrite: I shall visit you tomorrow, said Kato.
Option_A: Kato said that he will visit me tomorrow.
Option_B: Kato said that he would visit me the following day.
Option_C: Kato said that I should visit him the following day.
Option_D: Kato said he shall visit me the next day.
Detailed_Solution: 'I' becomes 'he', 'shall' becomes 'would', and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the following day'.

Question_Text: Rewrite: Are you coming? asked Otim.
Option_A: Otim asked if I was coming.
Option_B: Otim asked that am I coming.
Option_C: Otim asked whether are you coming.
Option_D: Otim wanted to know am I coming.
Detailed_Solution: Questions starting with helping verbs use 'if' or 'whether' as a connector.

Question_Text: Rewrite: Go to the garden, said mother.
Option_A: Mother said I go to the garden.
Option_B: Mother told me to go to the garden.
Option_C: Mother said to me go to the garden.
Option_D: Mother ordered that I go to the garden.
Detailed_Solution: Commands use the 'told/ordered + to + verb' structure.

Question_Text: Rewrite: Where is your report card? asked dad.
Option_A: Dad asked where my report card was.
Option_B: Dad asked where was my report card.
Option_C: Dad wanted to know where is my report card.
Option_D: Dad asked that where my report card was.
Detailed_Solution: In reported questions, the verb 'was' comes AFTER the subject.

Question_Text: Rewrite: We have been playing here, said the boys.
Option_A: The boys said they had been playing there.
Option_B: The boys said that we have been playing there.
Option_C: The boys said that they were playing here.
Option_D: The boys said they have been playing there.
Detailed_Solution: 'We' becomes 'they', 'have been' becomes 'had been', and 'here' becomes 'there'.

Question_Text: Rewrite: Don't make noise, said the teacher.
Option_A: The teacher said don't make noise.
Option_B: The teacher told us not to make noise.
Option_C: The teacher said that we don't make noise.
Option_D: The teacher asked us to not make noise.
Detailed_Solution: Negative commands use 'not to' followed by the verb.

Question_Text: Rewrite: I didn't see the bus, said Mary.
Option_A: Mary said that she didn't see the bus.
Option_B: Mary said that she hadn't seen the bus.
Option_C: Mary said that I hadn't seen the bus.
Option_D: Mary said that she hasn't seen the bus.
Detailed_Solution: Past simple 'didn't see' shifts to past perfect 'hadn't seen'.

Question_Text: Rewrite: I am late, said the boy. (Begin: The boy said... )
Option_A: The boy said he is late.
Option_B: The boy said that he was late.
Option_C: The boy said I was late.
Option_D: The boy said that he is late.
Detailed_Solution: Standard transformation: pronoun 'he', connector 'that', and past tense 'was'.

Question_Text: Rewrite: We shall leave next week, said the aunt.
Option_A: The aunt said that they should leave the following week.
Option_B: The aunt said that we would leave next week.
Option_C: The aunt said that they will leave the next week.
Option_D: The aunt said she would leave the following week.
Detailed_Solution: 'We' becomes 'they', 'shall' becomes 'should/would', 'next week' becomes 'the following week'.

Question_Text: Rewrite: The sun rises in the East, said the man.
Option_A: The man said that the sun rose in the East.
Option_B: The man said that the sun rises in the East.
Option_C: The man said the sun was rising in the East.
Option_D: The man said that the sun had risen in the East.
Detailed_Solution: Universal truths (like the sun rising) stay in the present tense.

Question_Text: Which adjective comes first in the NOSHACOMPAN rule?
Detailed_Solution: 'N' stands for Number (e.g., one, two, many), which always starts the sequence.

Question_Text: Choose the correct order: He bought _________ mangoes.
Detailed_Solution: Number (three) must come before Opinion (sweet).

Question_Text: Manya has a _________ bag.
Detailed_Solution: Size (big) must come before Origin (Ugandan).

Question_Text: She wore a _________ dress.
Detailed_Solution: Opinion (beautiful) must come before Colour (red).

Question_Text: Identify the material adjective in this list: _________.
Detailed_Solution: 'Wooden' describes the material the object is made of.

Question_Text: Which word describes an 'Opinion'?
Detailed_Solution: 'Smart' is an opinion; what one person thinks is smart, another may not.

Question_Text: We used a _________ table.
Detailed_Solution: Colour (white) must come before Material (plastic).

Question_Text: I saw _________ boys.
Detailed_Solution: Number (two) comes before Opinion (smart).

Question_Text: The dog is _________.
Detailed_Solution: Size (big) comes before Colour (black).

Question_Text: Kiki has a _________ kitten.
Detailed_Solution: Size (small) comes before Age (new).

Question_Text: Choose the correct order: She bought _________ shoes.
Detailed_Solution: Correct order: Age (new), Colour (black), Material (leather).

Question_Text: It was a _________ day.
Detailed_Solution: Opinion (hot) comes before secondary descriptions like weather (sunny).

Question_Text: Manya found a _________ coin.
Detailed_Solution: Size (small) comes before Shape (round) and Material (gold).

Question_Text: The teacher used a _________ stick.
Detailed_Solution: Size (long), Material (wooden), Purpose (walking).

Question_Text: We visited a _________ village.
Detailed_Solution: Opinion (quiet) comes before Size (small) and Location/Origin (rural).

Question_Text: She carried a _________ basket.
Detailed_Solution: Size (large), Origin (Ugandan), and 'woven' acts as material/type.

Question_Text: Choose the best arrangement: _________.
Detailed_Solution: Opinion/Shape (fat), Age (old), Colour (black).

Question_Text: He is a _________ player.
Detailed_Solution: Size (tall), Age (young), Origin (Kenyan).

Question_Text: They live in a _________ house.
Detailed_Solution: Size (big) comes before Age (modern) and Material (stone).

Question_Text: Which category does 'British' fall under in NOSHACOMPAN?
Detailed_Solution: 'British' describes the country of origin.

Question_Text: Arrange these adjectives: (Ugandan, two, beautiful, small, new).
Detailed_Solution: Number (two), Opinion (beautiful), Size (small), Age (new), Origin (Ugandan).

Question_Text: Rewrite as a single sentence: I have a ruler. It is plastic. It is nice. It is long.
Option_A: I have a long plastic nice ruler.
Option_B: I have a nice long plastic ruler.
Option_C: I have a plastic nice long ruler.
Option_D: I have a nice plastic long ruler.
Detailed_Solution: Opinion (nice), Size (long), Material (plastic).

Question_Text: Join these: The girl is brown. She is beautiful. She is tall. She is Ugandan.
Option_A: The beautiful tall brown Ugandan girl.
Option_B: The Ugandan beautiful tall brown girl.
Option_C: The tall beautiful brown Ugandan girl.
Option_D: The beautiful brown tall Ugandan girl
Detailed_Solution: Opinion (beautiful), Size (tall), Colour (brown), Origin (Ugandan).

Question_Text: What is the correct sequence for: (square, blue, large, wooden, one).
Detailed_Solution: Number (one), Size (large), Shape (square), Colour (blue), Material (wooden).

Question_Text: Correct the order: He bought a (cooking, new, metal, small) pot.
Option_A: A new small metal cooking pot
Option_B: A small new metal cooking pot
Option_C: A metal small new cooking pot
Option_D: A small metal new cooking pot
Detailed_Solution: Size (small), Age (new), Material (metal), Purpose (cooking).

Question_Text: Which sentence uses the correct order of adjectives?
Detailed_Solution: Number (three), Size (big), Age (old).

Question_Text: Identify the 'Purpose' adjective in: 'A heavy brown leather traveling bag'.
Detailed_Solution: 'Traveling' describes what the bag is used for (the purpose).

Question_Text: Join: I saw a snake. It was thin. It was long. It was green. It was scary.
Option_A: I saw a scary long thin green snake.
Option_B: I saw a long thin green scary snake.
Option_C: I saw a green long thin scary snake.
Option_D: I saw a scary green long thin snake.
Detailed_Solution: Opinion (scary), Size (long), Shape (thin), Colour (green).

Question_Text: Arrange these: (rectangular, Holland, multicolored, the) mat.
Detailed_Solution: Opinion/Colour (multicolored), Shape (rectangular), Origin (Holland).

Question_Text: Correct the order: (small, oval, pink, five) tablets.
Detailed_Solution: Number (five), Size (small), Shape (oval), Colour (pink).

Question_Text: In the passive voice for continuous actions, we must add the word ________.
Detailed_Solution: The word 'being' is required to show that the action is still going on in the passive voice.

Question_Text: What is the past participle (V3) of the verb 'sweep'?
Detailed_Solution: 'Swept' is the correct V3 form used in passive voice.

Question_Text: Identify the object in: 'The girls are peeling matooke.'
Detailed_Solution: The object is the thing receiving the action (matooke).

Question_Text: The cow is ________ milked by Manya.
Detailed_Solution: The formula for present continuous passive is is/are + being + V3.

Question_Text: Complete: The floor is being ________ (mop) by Kiki.
Detailed_Solution: Passive voice always uses the past participle (V3) of the main verb.

Question_Text: Active: Tom helps me. Passive: I ________ helped by Tom.
Detailed_Solution: The pronoun 'I' always takes the helping verb 'am'.

Question_Text: Which word shows that a person is doing the action?
Detailed_Solution: We use 'by' to introduce the 'doer' in a passive sentence.

Question_Text: What is the V3 of 'eat'?
Detailed_Solution: 'Eaten' is the correct past participle for the passive voice.

Question_Text: Passive: The compound is ________ cleaned.
Detailed_Solution: 'Being' is the indicator for continuous tense in passive voice.

Question_Text: Complete: Biko ________ eating mangoes. (Active)
Detailed_Solution: Biko is a singular subject, so we use 'is' in the active voice.

Question_Text: The room is ________ swept by the boys.
Detailed_Solution: Even if the 'doers' (boys) are plural, the verb 'is' matches the singular object 'room'.

Question_Text: Mangoes ________ being eaten by the children.
Detailed_Solution: 'Mangoes' is plural, so it requires the plural helping verb 'are'.

Question_Text: Identify the correct passive sentence.
Detailed_Solution: Rung is the V3 of ring. The sentence needs 'is being' for continuous.

Question_Text: The cows are being ________ (milk) now.
Detailed_Solution: V3 of 'milk' is 'milked'.

Question_Text: Active: We are reading books. Passive: Books are ________ read.
Detailed_Solution: Continuous passive must have 'being'.

Question_Text: The teacher ________ marking our books.
Detailed_Solution: Teacher is singular, so the active voice uses 'is'.

Question_Text: Passive: New skills are being ________ (learn) by pupils.
Detailed_Solution: Learnt (or learned) is the V3 of learn.

Question_Text: Active: Mother is cooking rice. Passive: Rice is being ________ by mother.
Detailed_Solution: Use 'is being' + V3 'cooked'.

Question_Text: Which sentence is in the passive voice?
Detailed_Solution: 'Being driven' indicates a passive structure.

Question_Text: The letters are being ________ (send) by pen-pals.
Detailed_Solution: Sent is the V3 of send.

Question_Text: Change to Passive: 'The maid is peeling matooke.'
Option_A: Matooke is peeling by the maid.
Option_B: Matooke is being peeled by the maid.
Option_C: Matooke are being peeled by the maid.
Option_D: The maid is being peeled by matooke.
Detailed_Solution: Matooke is an uncountable/singular noun, so use 'is being' + V3 'peeled'.

Question_Text: Change to Passive: 'The boys are cleaning the compound.'
Option_A: The compound is being cleaned by the boys.
Option_B: The compound are being cleaned by the boys.
Option_C: The boys are being cleaned by the compound.
Option_D: The compound is cleaned by the boys.
Detailed_Solution: Compound is singular, so use 'is being' even though 'boys' is plural.

Question_Text: Change to Passive: 'Someone is ringing the bell.'
Option_A: Someone is being rung by the bell.
Option_B: The bell is being rung by someone.
Option_D: The bell is rung by someone.
Detailed_Solution: TRAP: In PLE, vague subjects like 'someone' or 'people' are dropped in passive voice.

Question_Text: Change to Passive: 'The herdsman milks the cows.'
Option_B: The cows are being milked by the herdsman.
Option_C: The cows are milked by the herdsman.
Detailed_Solution: TRAP: This is Present Simple (milks), not Continuous. Do not use 'being' here!

Question_Text: Change to Active: 'A letter is being written by Jane.'
Detailed_Solution: Continuous passive 'is being written' moves to active 'is writing'.

Question_Text: Change to Passive: 'The girls are weaving nice baskets.'
Option_A: Nice baskets are being woven by the girls.
Option_B: Nice baskets is being woven by the girls.
Option_C: The girls are being woven into baskets.
Option_D: Nice baskets were being woven by the girls.
Detailed_Solution: 'Baskets' is plural, so use 'are being'. V3 of weave is 'woven'.

Question_Text: Change to Passive: 'Our parents are organizing birthday parties.'
Option_B: Birthday parties are being organized by our parents.
Option_C: Birthday parties were organized by our parents.
Detailed_Solution: Plural object 'parties' takes 'are being'.

Question_Text: Which sentence correctly drops the vague subject?
Option_A: Bread is being eaten by people.
Option_C: People are being eaten by bread.
Detailed_Solution: When 'people' or 'someone' is the subject, omit them in the passive voice.

Question_Text: Change to Passive: 'They are reading newspapers.'
Option_B: Newspapers were being read by them.
Detailed_Solution: Plural 'newspapers' takes 'are being'. Drop 'them' as it is a vague pronoun.

Question_Text: What happens to the verb 'is' when the object is plural?
Detailed_Solution: The helping verb must always agree with the new subject (the object of the active sentence).

Question_Text: We use since to show ________.
Option_C: a specific starting point in time
Detailed_Solution: 'Since' marks the exact moment an action began (e.g., Since 8:00 AM).

Question_Text: We use for to show ________.
Option_B: a period or length of time
Detailed_Solution: 'For' is used when we mention how long an action has lasted (e.g., For two hours).

Question_Text: Manya has been in the village ________ Monday.
Detailed_Solution: Monday is a specific point in time, so we use 'since'.

Question_Text: Kiki has slept ________ three hours.
Detailed_Solution: 'Three hours' is a duration or period of time, so 'for' is correct.

Question_Text: I haven't written to my pen-pal ________ January.
Detailed_Solution: January is a specific month (starting point), requiring 'since'.

Question_Text: They have stayed up-country ________ a month.
Detailed_Solution: 'A month' is a length of time, so we use 'for'.

Question_Text: The holiday has lasted ________ two weeks.
Detailed_Solution: 'Two weeks' describes the duration of the holiday.

Question_Text: Polly has lived here ________ 2020.
Detailed_Solution: A specific year like 2020 is a starting point, so use 'since'.

Question_Text: We have been waiting for the bus ________ morning.
Detailed_Solution: 'Morning' is a point in the day, so 'since' is the correct preposition.

Question_Text: It has been raining ________ a long time.
Detailed_Solution: 'A long time' is a general period of duration, requiring 'for'.

Question_Text: He has not visited the post office ________ five years.
Detailed_Solution: 'Five years' is a period of time. Use 'for'.

Question_Text: Manya has been waddling ________ he was a duckling.
Detailed_Solution: A clause like 'he was a duckling' describes a specific point in his life/time.

Question_Text: The teacher has been in the classroom ________ 9:00 AM.
Detailed_Solution: 9:00 AM is a precise starting point on the clock.

Question_Text: I have known my pen-pal ________ many years.
Detailed_Solution: 'Many years' is a duration of time.

Question_Text: Kiki has been on the farm ________ a fortnight.
Detailed_Solution: A 'fortnight' means two weeks, which is a period of time. Use 'for'.

Question_Text: The candidates have been revising ________ last term.
Detailed_Solution: 'Last term' is a specific point in the school calendar.

Question_Text: I have been in this school ________ three years.
Detailed_Solution: Three years is a duration. 'Since' would require a year like '2021'.

Question_Text: It is a year ________ I last saw Mr. Musoke.
Detailed_Solution: In the structure 'It is [time] since...', 'since' is the only correct linker.

Question_Text: We have played football ________ midday.
Detailed_Solution: 'Midday' is a point in time (12:00 PM).

Question_Text: She has been cooking ________ an hour.
Detailed_Solution: 'An hour' is a 60-minute duration.

Question_Text: Join: I joined this school in 2020. I am still here. (Use: ...since...)
Option_A: I am in this school for 2020.
Option_B: I have been in this school since 2020.
Option_D: I am being in this school since 2020.
Detailed_Solution: To join these, use the Present Perfect ('have been') + 'since' + the starting year.

Question_Text: Rewrite: It is a year since I saw him. (Begin: I haven't...)
Option_A: I haven't seen him since a year.
Option_B: I haven't seen him for a year.
Option_C: I haven't seen him since last year.
Option_D: I haven't seen him for last year.
Detailed_Solution: When rewriting 'It is a year since...', the duration 'a year' must follow 'for'.

Question_Text: Rewrite: We started the party at 2:00 PM. It is now 5:00 PM.
Option_A: We have had the party since three hours.
Option_B: We have had the party since 2:00 PM.
Option_C: We have the party for 2:00 PM.
Option_D: We had the party since 2:00 PM.
Detailed_Solution: The action started at a point (2:00 PM) and continues, so use 'since' with the start time.

Question_Text: Rewrite: Okello visited the post office five years ago. (Use: ...for...)
Option_A: Okello has not visited the post office for five years.
Option_B: Okello visited the post office for five years.
Option_C: Okello is not at the post office since five years.
Option_D: Okello has visited the post office since five years.
Detailed_Solution: To show the time passed since the last visit, use the negative present perfect + 'for' + duration.

Question_Text: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
Option_A: I haven't met him, since January.
Option_B: I haven't met him since January.
Option_C: I haven't met him; since January.
Option_D: I haven't, met him since January.
Detailed_Solution: Prepositional phrases at the end of a sentence do not need a comma.

Question_Text: Join: The rain started in the morning. It is still raining. (Use: ...since...)
Option_C: It has been raining since morning.
Detailed_Solution: Use the Present Perfect Continuous ('has been raining') to show an action continuing from a point.

Question_Text: Rewrite: I last wrote a letter in 2010. (Begin: I haven't...)
Option_A: I haven't written a letter for 2010.
Option_B: I haven't written a letter since 2010.
Option_C: I haven't wrote a letter since 2010.
Option_D: I haven't been writing a letter for 2010.
Detailed_Solution: Ensure the use of the past participle 'written' and the point preposition 'since'.

Question_Text: The post master has been talking to us ________ 2:00 PM.
Detailed_Solution: Clock time is always a specific point. Use 'since'.

Question_Text: Which word is the opposite of 'commenced'?
Detailed_Solution: Commence means start; the opposite is end or concluded.

Question_Text: Join: He began singing at 6:00 AM. It is now midday. (Use: ...for...)
Option_A: He has been singing since six hours.
Option_B: He has been singing for six hours.
Option_C: He is singing for six hours.
Option_D: He was singing for six hours.
Detailed_Solution: Midday (12:00) minus 6:00 AM = 6 hours. Use 'for' for the duration.
